analysis.one_liner: Exempts state-regulated insurers from Consumer Bureau enforcement of financial rules.
analysis.headline: The bill died in committee: referred to the Senate Banking Committee in January 2024, it never received a committee or floor vote before the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would bar the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau from enforcing federal consumer financial laws against insurance companies that are already regulated by a state insurance regulator, and would force the bureau to read its remaining authority over such companies as narrowly as possible. It would also instruct courts and the bureau to favor state insurance regulators when interpreting enforcement power. The bill never got a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote, and expired when the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Insurance companies and other businesses 'engaged in the business of insurance' would gain, because they could no longer face CFPB enforcement actions over consumer financial products such as annuities, credit insurance, or other insurance-linked financial products. They would be answerable only to state insurance regulators, whose rules and enforcement capacity vary widely from state to state.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Insurance companies and insurance-linked financial firms

how_it_helps.text: The bill prohibits the CFPB from enforcing federal consumer financial law against any person regulated by a state insurance regulator to the extent that person is engaged in the business of insurance.
For people otherwise subject to the bureau's authority, the bill requires the bureau to construe its enforcement powers narrowly when the person is engaged in the business of insurance.

The bill adds a rule of construction that federal consumer financial enforcement must be broadly read in favor of state insurance regulator authority, replacing the prior provision describing activities outside bureau reach.

analysis.who_pays: Consumers who buy insurance-linked financial products would lose a federal backstop: if a company sold them an annuity, credit insurance, or another product and violated federal consumer financial law, the CFPB could no longer pursue the case. They would be left to whatever remedies their state insurance regulator provides, and state oversight of consumer financial protection varies a great deal.

drawbacks.text: State insurance regulators have long supervised insurance, but their primary mission and resources differ from the CFPB's consumer-protection mandate, so shifting enforcement entirely to them could leave gaps in oversight of insurance-linked financial products.

The bill does not just remove bureau enforcement; it also requires the bureau to read any remaining authority over insurance businesses narrowly and to broadly favor state regulator authority, which could weaken enforcement even under existing federal consumer laws those firms remain subject to.

A supporter's honest cost-benefit case: supporters argue the bill simply prevents duplicate federal and state regulation of a sector states have regulated for decades, and that the cost to consumers is theoretical if state regulators do their jobs. The trade-off is real either way.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit to insurers is clear and immediate: fewer federal enforcement actions and a narrower reading of federal consumer laws. The benefit to consumers is harder to see — mainly the argument that one regulator (the state) is better than two. The cost falls on consumers, who would depend entirely on state insurance regulators of uneven strength for protection against financial abuses in insurance products. Given that the bureau would also be forced to construe its remaining authority narrowly, the scales tip toward industry.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Banking Committee the day it was introduced and the committee never took it up, so it expired when the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Senator Tim Scott (R-SC) introduced the bill with Senator Joe Manchin (D-WV) on January 16, 2024.
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs the same day.
The complete action history shows no further action: no hearing, no committee vote, and no floor vote in the Senate or House.
The 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, so the bill died without a vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Consumers and the CFPB's enforcement authority are better off in the narrow sense that nothing changed: insurance businesses selling consumer financial products remain subject to federal consumer financial enforcement as before. Insurers gained nothing, having sought an exemption from bureau enforcement.

for.name: Sen. Tim Scott
for.role: U.S. Senator from South Carolina (Ranking Member, Senate Banking Committee)
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to limit CFPB enforcement authority over state-regulated insurance businesses.

for.name: Sen. Joe Manchin
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored and co-introduced the bill, making it a bipartisan sponsorship.

against.name: Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee
against.role: Committee of referral (Chair Sherrod Brown, D-OH)
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral — no hearing, no markup, no committee vote — leaving it to expire.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsorship was bipartisan (one Republican and one Democrat), and the bill drew no recorded floor opposition because it never reached a vote; with only two sponsors and no committee action, no partisan pattern in support or opposition can be read from the record.

industries.note: The bill would exempt state-regulated insurance businesses from CFPB enforcement of federal consumer financial laws and force narrow construction of any remaining federal authority. Insurers would face less federal oversight of insurance-linked financial products, and consumers would lose a federal backstop for complaints.

The bill would make state insurance regulators the sole primary enforcer for insurance businesses and instruct that federal enforcement be read broadly in their favor. Their authority would grow, though their consumer-protection capacity varies by state.
